--- # This chapter has REAL runnable cells, so it needs the knitr engine, the # include line below, and the quarto-live extension in _extensions/. # To go back to a book that renders with nothing installed, see "Going back". engine: knitr --- ::: {.cell} ::: # Code students can run in the browser {#sec-webr} This is the newest of the interactive options, and for a course that teaches programming it is the most useful. **The student edits your code and presses Run, and it executes in their browser** — no R installed, no server, no accounts, no logins that break in week 3. ## What it looks like Both cells below are real. Each is an editor with **Run Code** and **Start Over** buttons: change anything, run it again, and reset it when you have made a mess. ::: {.cell} ```{webr} for (x in 1:5) { print(10 + x) } ``` ::: Small on purpose: the very first cell on a page has to download R itself, so a three-line example gets the student to their first **Run Code** quickly. Once webR is loaded, everything else on the page is instant. The second cell is a real model — change `d` to `0.9` and the paracetamol takes far longer to clear: ::: {.cell caption='Paracetamol in de bloedbaan' min-lines='12'} ```{webr} #| caption: Paracetamol in de bloedbaan #| min-lines: 12 p <- 400 # hoeveelheid paracetamol d <- 0.7 # afname (d van decay) for (i in 1:100) { if (runif(1) < 0.1) { # nieuwe pil met kans 0.1 p[i] <- p[i] + 400 } p[i+1] <- p[i] * d } plot(p, type = 'l', lwd = 2, col = "#C00A35", xlab = "Tijd (uren)", ylab = "Paracetamol (mg)") ``` ::: ::: {.callout-note} ## These two are live Press **Run Code**. The first cell has to fetch R itself, so give it a few seconds; after that everything on the page is instant. @sec-webr-install explains how this was set up, and how to switch it back off. ::: ## Where this sits among the other options | Option | Who wrote the code | Can the student change it? | Where does it run | |---|---|---|---| | External iframe (@sec-iframes) | Someone else | Only what the tool allows | Their server | | Internal applet (@sec-ai) | You, once | No — sliders only | The student's browser | | **Runnable code cell** | **You** | **Yes, any of it** | **The student's browser** | : The three kinds of interactive content. {#tbl-interactive} An applet is the right choice when you want a student to *explore a relationship*. A runnable code cell is right when you want them to *write the code*. ## Installing it {#sec-webr-install} The extension is [**Quarto Live**](https://r-wasm.github.io/quarto-live/), and installing it is the one moment in this guide that needs a terminal. It is one command, run once per project. ::: {.callout-tip} ## Step by step, in RStudio 1. Open the project (`File → Open Project`, or double-click its `.Rproj`). 2. Click the **Terminal** tab — bottom-left pane, next to Console. 3. **Check where you are.** Type `pwd` and press Enter. It must print your project folder. If it prints your home folder instead, move there first: ```{=html} 
cd ~/Dropbox/…/YourBookFolder
``` 4. Now install: ```{=html} 
quarto add r-wasm/quarto-live
``` 5. It asks whether you trust the authors — press **Y**, Enter. It may ask a second time to confirm; **Y** again. 6. Check it worked: a folder `_extensions/r-wasm/live/` should now exist in the project. In RStudio's Files pane you may need the **More → Show Hidden Files** option to see it. ::: ::: {.callout-warning} ## The mistake that costs ten minutes `quarto add` installs into **whatever folder the Terminal is currently in**, not into the project you have open in RStudio. Those are usually the same thing, but not always — a Terminal that opened in your home folder will cheerfully create `_extensions` there, report success, and leave your book exactly as broken as before. That is what step 3 is for. If it has already happened, just drag the stray `_extensions` folder into your project. ::: **Commit the `_extensions/` folder to Git** along with everything else. Then a colleague who clones the book does not have to install anything, and neither does a build server. ## Switching the book over Two edits, both one line. **In `_quarto.yml`,** change the html format to `live-html`: ```{=html} 
format:
  live-html:          # was: html
    theme: [cosmo, uu.scss]
    toc: true
``` `live-html` is ordinary `html` with the WebAssembly machinery added, so everything else — the theme, the sidebar, cross-references — carries on unchanged. **At the top of every chapter that has a live cell**, immediately below the closing `---` of the YAML header: ```{=html} 
{{< include ./_extensions/r-wasm/live/_knitr.qmd >}}
``` That line registers `webr` as an engine that knitr recognises, and it is needed whenever your book runs R chunks anywhere — which it almost certainly does. Miss it and Quarto stops with *"Include directive failed"*; miss the `live-html` change and the cells render as ordinary dead code blocks with no Run button. This chapter has both — look at its source. ::: {.callout-note} ## Going back Reverse the same two edits: `live-html` back to `html`, delete the include line, and put `engine: markdown` in the chapter header so Quarto stops looking for something to execute. The book then renders on any machine with no extension installed, which is what you want before handing it to a colleague who has not installed anything. ::: ## Writing a cell A live R cell is a `{webr}` block. That is the whole syntax — you write this: ```{=html} 
```{webr}
plot(sin(seq(0, 4 * pi, 0.1)), type = 'l', lwd = 2, col = "#C00A35")
```
``` …and your students get this: ::: {.cell} ```{webr} plot(sin(seq(0, 4 * pi, 0.1)), type = 'l', lwd = 2, col = "#C00A35") ``` ::: Source above, result below — the same three backticks either way. Every example from here on is shown in that pair. ## Cell options Options go at the top of the cell, `#|` style, exactly like ordinary chunks — the cell above uses `caption` and `min-lines`. | Option | Effect | |---|---| | `autorun: true` | run once as the page loads, so the student sees output before touching anything | | `edit: false` | show and run it, but do not let them change it | | `runbutton: false` | no Run button — pair with `autorun` for a live demo | | `startover: false` | remove the reset button | | `persist: true` | remember the student's edits in their browser across reloads | | `min-lines`, `max-lines` | control the height of the editor box | | `timelimit: 10` | seconds before a runaway loop is stopped (default 30) | | `caption: "Try changing d"` | a title on the cell | | `include: false` | run it invisibly — for setup code the student should not see | : Live cell options. {#tbl-live-options} Options change the cell quite a lot. This one is set to run itself on page load and refuse edits — a live demonstration rather than an exercise: ```{=html} 
```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| edit: false
#| caption: Exponentiële versus logistische groei
```
``` ::: {.cell autorun='true' edit='false' caption='Exponentiële versus logistische groei'} ```{webr} #| autorun: true #| edit: false #| caption: Exponentiële versus logistische groei t <- 0:40 exponential <- 2 * exp(0.12 * t) logistic <- 100 / (1 + 49 * exp(-0.12 * t)) plot(t, logistic, type = 'l', lwd = 2, col = "#C00A35", ylim = c(0, 120), xlab = "tijd", ylab = "N") lines(t, exponential, lwd = 2, lty = 2, col = "#001240") legend("topleft", c("logistisch", "exponentieel"), col = c("#C00A35", "#001240"), lty = c(1, 2), lwd = 2, bty = "n") ``` ::: Notice there is no Run button and no editor — it simply appeared. Compare it with the cells at the top of the chapter, which have both. ::: {.callout-warning} ## Live cells need a web *server* — and Render alone does not start one Open `docs/index.html` straight off your disk and the cells appear but stay dead: the editor never initialises, because browsers refuse to start the WebAssembly worker over a `file://` address. It looks exactly like a broken install, and it is not. **Render** builds the book but does not necessarily serve it. Worse, once the format is `live-html` RStudio no longer recognises it as something it knows how to preview, so the Render button quietly stops opening a preview window at all — it prints *"Output created: docs/index.html"* and nothing appears. To see live cells locally, start a server yourself. In the **Terminal** tab, from the project folder: ```{=html} 
quarto preview
``` That builds the book, serves it at a `http://localhost:####` address, opens your browser at it, and re-renders whenever you save. Stop it with Ctrl+C. If it opens inside RStudio's Viewer pane rather than a real browser, click the *Show in new window* icon — the Viewer is a cut-down browser and WebAssembly is exactly the sort of thing it is bad at. Published to GitHub Pages the book is served over `https://`, so students never meet any of this. ::: ::: {.callout-tip} ## The setup-cell pattern Put data loading and library calls in an `include: false` cell at the top of the chapter. State carries between cells on the same page, so the student's cell can then be three lines about the actual idea instead of fifteen lines of boilerplate. ::: ## Packages Packages must be declared in the YAML so they are fetched when the page loads: ```{=html} 
webr:
  packages:
    - dplyr
    - ggplot2
``` ::: {.callout-warning} ## Not every package exists in WebAssembly An R package has to have been compiled for WebAssembly. Most of the common ones are, at [repo.r-wasm.org](https://repo.r-wasm.org), and R-universe builds WebAssembly versions automatically — add a `repos:` key to pull from one. But anything wrapping compiled C or Fortran that nobody has ported will simply not be there. **Check the packages you need before you rewrite a practical around this.** Python has the same limitation, with a different list — see @sec-webr-python. Every live cell in this chapter uses only base R or the Python standard library, deliberately. ::: ## The same trick for Python {#sec-webr-python} There is nothing to install. The extension you already added ships **Pyodide** — CPython compiled to WebAssembly — alongside webR, and the include line at the top of this chapter registers both engines. Write `{pyodide}` instead of `{webr}` and it simply works: ```{=html} 
```{pyodide}
#| caption: Exponentiële groei
r, N = 0.12, 2.0
for t in range(10):
    print(f"t = {t:2d}   N = {N:6.2f}")
    N = N * (1 + r)
```
``` Which gives you a Python editor, with its own Run Code button: ::: {.cell caption='Exponentile groei'} ```{pyodide} #| caption: Exponentiële groei r, N = 0.12, 2.0 for t in range(10): print(f"t = {t:2d} N = {N:6.2f}") N = N * (1 + r) ``` ::: Packages work the same way, under their own key: ```{=html} 
webr:
  packages: [dplyr, ggplot2]
pyodide:
  packages: [numpy, matplotlib]
``` Pyodide ships the scientific stack, and `micropip` can fetch pure-Python wheels from PyPI — but not packages whose compiled parts have never been built for WebAssembly. Same caveat as R, different list. ::: {.callout-warning} ## One page, two runtimes This page now loads **both** webR and Pyodide, because it has cells of both kinds. That is roughly double the first-load cost, and this chapter only does it to show you that it works. In a real course book, keep a page to one language unless you genuinely need both. Where you do — an introductory course where half the room knows R and half knows Python — a `::: {.panel-tabset}` with an R cell in one tab and a Python cell in the other is the tidy way to do it. ::: ## What it costs {#sec-webr-cost} ::: {.callout-important} ## The first cell on a page is slow Loading webR means downloading R itself — tens of megabytes. Expect a few seconds on a good connection and rather longer on eduroam in a full lecture hall. After that it is fast, and it is cached for the rest of the session. Two things help: put an `autorun: true` cell early on so the download starts while the student is still reading, and do not scatter live cells across twenty chapters when three practical pages would do. ::: Two more limits worth knowing before you commit a practical to this: - **No files and no network.** The browser sandbox means no reading from the student's disk and no `download.file()`. Ship data inside the page, or as a URL the extension is configured to fetch. - **It is not a replacement for teaching them to install R.** If the course outcome is "can run an analysis on their own laptop", they still have to install it. This is for the explaining, not for the doing. ## Does it work in the PDF? No — like everything else in this part of the book, a live cell needs a browser. Wrap it the way @sec-pdf describes: the live version inside `::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}`, and for the PDF a plain non-executing code block showing the same code, so the printed book still has something to read. ## Writing *about* live cells There is a trap here, and this chapter walks into it deliberately so you do not have to. Quarto picks an engine per file by scanning the raw text for cell fences, *before* it parses any markdown. A ```` ```{webr} ```` fence therefore counts even when you only meant to show it as an example — nesting it inside a bigger code block, indenting it, or adding backticks makes no difference. In a book with no live cells at all, that alone is enough to make Quarto demand a Python kernel and stop with: ```{=html} 
Starting python3 kernel...
Jupyter is not available in this Python installation.
``` The syntax examples on this page are therefore written as raw HTML blocks rather than fenced ones — look at the source. They still get a copy button, Quarto never sees a fence at all, and it is what lets this chapter print a cell's source and *run that same cell* directly underneath. ::: {.callout-tip} ## If you only want to *describe* live cells A chapter that shows the syntax but runs nothing needs neither the extension nor the include. Put `engine: markdown` in its YAML header and Quarto will stop looking for something to execute. :::
